anchor.title: SequenceMatrix: concatenation software for the fast assembly of multi-gene datasets with character set and codon information

claims.text: The citation is almost entirely methodological boilerplate: all 40 sampled citing papers use SequenceMatrix as a tool, and none use its data, argue with it, or extend it. Its single job in every case is concatenating separately aligned loci into a combined matrix.

The dominant user community is fungal taxonomy, where SequenceMatrix sits in a near-standardized pipeline for describing new species from ITS, LSU, SSU, rpb2 and tef1-α alignments — MycoKeys, IMA Fungus, Journal of Fungi and Mycobiology papers make up a large share of the sample.

The recurring workflow is trim-then-concatenate-then-infer: sequences assembled in SeqMan/BioEdit, aligned with MAFFT, trimmed with trimAl or Gblocks, concatenated in SequenceMatrix, then analyzed in RAxML/IQ-TREE and MrBayes with ModelFinder or MrModeltest.

Use extends well beyond fungi into animals, plants and even bacteria: primates, pseudoscorpions, tardigrades, crickets, sika deer, freshwater mussels, gastropods, birds, Bromeliaceae, Lamiaceae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa clinical isolates.

A notable second use is genome-scale rather than multi-locus: several papers concatenate protein-coding genes extracted from whole mitochondrial, chloroplast or organelle genomes, a scale the tool was not originally pitched at.

Stance is overwhelmingly neutral — a one-clause mention with no evaluation — and the few positive framings only praise the output (a "unified dataset", a "super matrix" for inferring relatedness) rather than the software itself. No paper in the sample critiques or benchmarks it.

Citation practice is loose in ways worth noting: versions span 1.7.6 through 1.9 with no rationale given for the choice, and one paper cites a self-contradictory "Sequence Matrix 1.9 v1.7.6", while another cites the paper only for format conversion to NEXUS rather than concatenation.

Despite the paper's emphasis on character-set and codon-position handling, the sampled passages rarely mention those features; where partitioning matters it is described separately, as in a partitioned analysis built from three concatenated single-locus datasets or in a supermatrix where missing sites are simply coded as missing data.

follow_ups: Do any citing papers actually exploit SequenceMatrix's codon/character-set export, or is it purely used as a concatenator?
Why is version use so scattered (1.7.6–1.9), and are newer versions cited for any functional reason?
In the genome-scale uses, how does SequenceMatrix compare to PhyloSuite or AMAS, which appear alongside it in some pipelines?
Is the fungal-taxonomy dominance a real usage pattern or an artifact of the sampling of 40 from 208 citing works?
How are papers handling missing data and partition files downstream — does SequenceMatrix's output feed ModelFinder partitions directly?

claims.text: Overwhelmingly, SequenceMatrix is cited as a routine utility rather than an object of discussion: 39 of 40 sampled citing works use it as a tool, and nearly all do the same single job — concatenating per-locus alignments into a combined multi-gene matrix.

The heaviest concentration of use is in fungal taxonomy, where SequenceMatrix (usually v1.7.8) is a fixed step in the standard species-description pipeline combining ITS, LSU, SSU, tef1-α, rpb2 and tub2 alignments.

It sits in a stable toolchain: alignment with MAFFT/MUSCLE/ClustalX, trimming with trimAl/Gblocks/BioEdit, then SequenceMatrix, then model selection (ModelFinder, PartitionFinder, MrModeltest) and tree inference in RAxML, IQ-TREE or MrBayes.

Use extends well beyond the taxonomic workflow it was written for, into mitogenomics and phylogenomics, where it concatenates 13 PCGs plus rRNAs into alternative matrices (PCG12, PCG12R, amino-acid) or dozens of plastid/orthologous genes.

A few citations fall outside phylogenetic systematics entirely: concatenating influenza A gene segments into codon-complete genomes, and building concatenated bacterial sequences (with 150 bp 'N' spacers) for a study of contamination in ethanol biorefineries.

Beyond concatenation, authors lean on secondary features — automatic filling of failed amplifications as missing data, gene- and codon-position partitioning, and even scanning matrices for mislabelled sequences as a QC step.

Stance is neutral-to-positive with no recorded criticism in the sample: one methods paper for fungal phylogeny explicitly endorses it as "a good choice" for multi-locus concatenation, and none of the sampled works compare against or contradict it.

Citation hygiene is sloppy in places: the software is variously named "Sequence Matrix", "SquenceMatrix" or "Sequence-Matrix", attributed as "Vaidya and Lohman 2011", and version numbers range from a nonexistent-sounding "version 7.8" and "v16.0" to 1.7.8, 1.8, 1.9 and 1.10 — suggesting many authors copy the citation forward without checking.

follow_ups: Do any citing works report concrete problems (GUI limits, matrix size ceilings, partition-file format errors) that the sampled passages missed?
How often is SequenceMatrix chosen over scriptable alternatives like catfasta2phyml, AMAS, or phyluce's concatenation, and do authors give reasons?
In the mitogenomic and phylogenomic cases, does concatenation with SequenceMatrix coexist with coalescent methods (ASTRAL) or replace them?
Is the widespread miscitation of version numbers traceable to a few highly copied methods sections in fungal taxonomy journals?
Has citation volume shifted since 2020 toward or away from concatenation-based supermatrix approaches?

claims.text: Overwhelmingly, SequenceMatrix is cited as a utility tool: 39 of 40 sampled citing works use it, and essentially all of them for one job — concatenating separately aligned loci into a combined supermatrix for phylogenetic analysis.

The citation is typically a single methods-section sentence with no evaluation, often naming only the version (1.7.8, 1.8, or 1.9), which suggests the tool is treated as infrastructure rather than something to justify.

It sits in a highly stereotyped pipeline: alignment with MAFFT or MUSCLE, trimming with GBlocks or trimAl, concatenation in SequenceMatrix, partitioning with PartitionFinder or ModelFinder, then RAxML/IQ-TREE/MrBayes.

Taxonomic breadth is striking and far beyond the insect-systematics context of the original paper — fungi, oomycetes, orchid and Vicia plastomes, primates, rodents, centipedes, copepods, spiders, nudibranchs, and marsupials all appear in the sample.

Several uses are microbial or genomic rather than classical multi-gene barcoding: concatenating MLST housekeeping genes for phytoplasma typing, building a ~1.09 Mb per-strain sequence from core-genome gene alignments in Xanthomonas, and stitching protein alignments from mitogenomes.

Its character-set and codon-partition features are exercised explicitly by some users — e.g. treating four mitochondrial protein-coding genes as one gene with three codon partitions, or exporting Nexus files for downstream partitioned analyses.

No sampled paper critiques or benchmarks against SequenceMatrix; the only non-use citation is BAD2matrix, which lists it among existing multilocus concatenators and argues such tools do not scale to phylogenomic-sized eukaryote datasets — an implicit scope limitation rather than a direct complaint.

One caveat for anyone tracing impact: at least one heavily cited user of the tool, a copepod order-level phylogeny, has been retracted, so citation counts include work whose conclusions were withdrawn even though the concatenation step itself was not at issue.

follow_ups: Do citing papers that use SequenceMatrix's indel/character-set coding features differ systematically from those using it only as a plain concatenator?
Has the citation rate shifted toward BAD2matrix, AMAS, or catfasta2phyml as datasets moved to phylogenomic scale after ~2020?
How many citing works report the version, and does version reporting correlate with journal or field?
In mycology specifically, has SequenceMatrix become a de facto requirement of the multi-locus species-description template?
Are there documented cases where concatenation-order or missing-data handling in SequenceMatrix affected published topologies?

claims.text: Across all three windows the citation does one thing: SequenceMatrix is named in a methods sentence as the tool that concatenated separately aligned loci into a combined supermatrix. Sampling is consistent — 39-40 of 40 citers in each window are tool uses, with no data reuse, no benchmarking, and no extension.

It is treated as infrastructure rather than a choice to justify: the typical passage gives only a version number and no evaluation, and the version cited drifts from 1.7.6 through 1.7.8, 1.8, 1.9 and 1.10 with no stated rationale.

The surrounding toolchain has been stable for over a decade: MAFFT or MUSCLE for alignment, trimAl/Gblocks/BioEdit for trimming, SequenceMatrix for concatenation, then PartitionFinder/ModelFinder/MrModeltest and RAxML, IQ-TREE or MrBayes.

What changed over time is the user base, not the usage. Earlier citation spans broad systematics (primates, rodents, centipedes, copepods, spiders, nudibranchs, orchid and Vicia plastomes), while the recent window is dominated by fungal taxonomy, where the tool is a fixed step in describing new species from ITS, LSU, SSU, tef1-α and rpb2 alignments in MycoKeys, IMA Fungus and Journal of Fungi.

A second drift is upward in scale: authors increasingly use it on genome-derived data — 13 mitochondrial PCGs in PCG12/PCG12R/amino-acid matrices, dozens of plastid or orthologous genes, core-genome alignments yielding ~1.09 Mb per Xanthomonas strain — well past the multi-gene barcoding scale the paper was pitched at.

Some citers exercise features beyond plain concatenation — automatic coding of failed amplifications as missing data, gene and codon-position character sets (e.g. four mitochondrial PCGs as one gene with three codon partitions), Nexus export, and even scanning matrices for mislabelled sequences as a QC step — but in the most recent window these features are rarely mentioned, despite being the paper's selling point.

Stance is neutral to mildly positive with essentially no criticism: one fungal-phylogeny methods paper calls it "a good choice" for multi-locus concatenation, and the few other evaluative phrases praise the output ("unified dataset", "super matrix") rather than the software. The closest thing to a complaint is BAD2matrix, which lists it among existing concatenators and argues such tools do not scale to phylogenomic-sized eukaryote datasets — a scope limit, not a defect claim.

Citation hygiene is poor and worth watching: the name appears as "Sequence Matrix", "SquenceMatrix" and "Sequence-Matrix", the attribution is sometimes flipped to "Vaidya and Lohman 2011", versions like "version 7.8", "v16.0" and the self-contradictory "Sequence Matrix 1.9 v1.7.6" appear, and at least one paper cites it only for NEXUS format conversion — signs the citation is being copied forward unchecked.

Two edge cases show the citation escaping phylogenetic systematics entirely: concatenating influenza A gene segments into codon-complete genomes, and joining bacterial sequences with 150 bp 'N' spacers to study contamination in ethanol biorefineries. A separate caveat for impact tracing is that at least one prominent user, a copepod order-level phylogeny, has been retracted.

follow_ups: Does the shift toward fungal taxonomy reflect real growth in that field's output, or displacement of SequenceMatrix by other concatenators (AMAS, catfasta2phyml, phyluce) in animal phylogenomics?
How many citers actually use the character-set/codon-partition output versus just the concatenated FASTA — can that be measured from deposited supplementary matrices?
Do the genome-scale users hit the practical limits BAD2matrix's scaling critique predicts, and do any report workarounds?
Where did the malformed version strings ('version 7.8', 'v16.0', '1.9 v1.7.6') originate — is a widely copied methods template propagating them?
Is there any published benchmark comparing SequenceMatrix against newer tools for correctness on missing data and partition bookkeeping?

W2611219129.title: The Complete Plastome Sequences of Four Orchid Species: Insights into the Evolution of the Orchidaceae and the Utility of Plastomic Mutational Hotspots

passages.section: Materials and Methods > Construction of Phylogenetic Trees
passages.text: In orchids, the loss of plastid ndh genes has independently occurred among different genera (Lin et al., 2015). The truncation or complete loss of ndh genes can lead to difficulties in alignment, caused by the high rates of nucleotide substitution or the presence of many deletions and insertions. Therefore, we only extracted sequences of 67 plastid protein-coding genes common to 53 orchids and eight other monocots (Supplementary Table S1) (without ndh genes). Sequence alignments were performed using MUSCLE. After removing all gaps and ambiguous sites, the alignments of the 67 genes were concatenated using SequenceMatrix 1.8 (Vaidya et al., 2011). The partitions of the 67 concatenated genes were analyzed using PartitionFinder v1.1.1 (Lanfear et al., 2012) and the result was incorporated into construction of maximum likelihood (ML) and Bayesian inference (BI) trees using RAxML 8.0.2 (Stamatakis, 2014) and MrBayes 3.2 (Ronquist et al., 2012), respectively. Fritillaria taipaiensis and Lilium longiflorum were designated as outgroups. The robustness of the ML tree was estimated using 1,000 bootstrap replicates. We performed two independent MCMC runs in analyses of the BI tree. Each run yielded one million generations. We collected one tree per 1,000 generations. The initial 25% of the collected trees were discarded as burn-in, and the remaining ones were used to estimate posterior probability.

W2749951673.title: RETRACTED ARTICLE: Molecular Phylogeny and Revision of Copepod Orders (Crustacea: Copepoda)

passages.section: Materials and Methods > DNA Extraction and Molecular Analyses
passages.text: DNA extraction from whole individuals were performed using 25–35 μL Chelex (InstaGene Matrix, Bio−Rad) according to the protocol of Estoup et al.35. From each DNA extract, 20–30 μL of the supernatant was separated from copepod’s voucher specimen, placed in a labeled sterile tube and stored at −20 °C for later DNA analysis. The remaining (generally intact) exoskeletons of the extracted individuals were transferred to glycerin on a glass slide and stored as a voucher for morphological identifications. Genes encoding the nuclear large (28S) and small (18S) subunits of rRNA, Histone 3 protein (H3) and mitochondrial protein cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI) were used for phylogenetic analysis. Amplification was performed using Illustra PuReTaq Ready−To−Go PCR Beads (GE Healthcare) or AccuStart PCR SuperMix (ThermoFisher Scientific) in a 25-μL volume containing 22 μL H2O or PCR SuperMix, 0.5 μL of each primer (10 pmol μL−1) and 2 μL of DNA template. PCR and sequencing primers used for each gene, the length of the amplified regions and the annealing temperature are specified in Supplementary Table S4. PCR products were checked by electrophoresis on a 1% agarose/TAE gel containing 1x GelRed. Forward and reverse sequences for each individual and gene were assembled and edited using Geneious (version 9.1.5 and 5.4.5 Biomatters; http://www.geneious.com). All sequences were searched against the GenBank nucleotide database using BLASTN36. Edited DNA sequences for four genes were separately aligned using MAFFT v7.017 under E-INS-i and G-INS-i algorithms37 and concatenated using SequenceMatrix 1.7.838. Alignments were further manually edited; regions with ambiguous alignment and an insertion present in seven parasitic poecilostome species (marked in Supplementary Table S3) were excluded from the matrix.

role.what_for: To concatenate aligned DNA sequences from four genes into a single matrix for phylogenetic analysis.
role.evidence_quote: Edited DNA sequences for four genes were separately aligned using MAFFT v7.017 under E-INS-i and G-INS-i algorithms37 and concatenated using SequenceMatrix 1.7.838.

passages.text: To obtain an accurate phylogeny of the genus Pseudomonas, we retrieved the nucleotide sequences of 55 housekeeping genes (supplementary table S1, Supplementary Material online) for 28 Pseudomonas genomes (supplementary fig. S1, Supplementary Material online) plus Azotobacter vinelandii from the Integrated Microbial Genomes database (Markowitz et al. 2012) using reciprocal BLAST to make sure of their orthology. Multiple alignments for all genes were obtained using MUSCLE (Edgar 2004) and afterwards trimmed with GBlocks (Castresana 2000) and concatenated with SequenceMatrix (Vaidya et al. 2011). The resulting supermatrix was then used to infer the nucleotide substitution model using JModelTest 2 (Darriba et al. 2012). A maximum-likelihood (ML) phylogenetic tree was then inferred assuming a GTR+G+I model with PHYML (Guindon et al. 2010). Additional trees inferred using Bayesian inference and Neighbor Joining as well as a ML tree obtained with a supermatrix of the protein sequences yielded identical topologies (data not shown). The relevant phylogeny for the eight strains in this study system was then manually extracted. Branch lengths are proportional to genetic distance and all nodes on this phylogeny are strongly supported with at least 99% confidence, as determined by an approximate log-likelihood ratio test (Furio V, Maclean RC, unpublished manuscript).

passages.text: Inferred amino acid sequences were aligned using MAFFT version 7 [49] and the resulting alignments were manually trimmed. Highly variable misaligned sections of several eukaryotic sequences, possibly results of sequencing errors, were removed from the alignment manually. The concatenated alignment was constructed from the single gene alignments using SequenceMatrix [50]. The final alignments can be downloaded from our web page: http://protistologie.cz/hampllab/NovakData.zip [51]. Phylogenetic inference was performed using substitution models suggested by ProtTest 2.4 server [52] – LG4X + Γ model. Maximum Likelihood trees were inferred using RAxML-HPC2 version 8 available on CIPRES [53], with 10 starting trees and also using IQ-TREE v1.4.2 [54] under the LG + C20 + F + G4 model for the single gene trees and LG + C40 + F + G4 model for concatenated datasets. The model that best fits the data was determined by IQ-TREE according to the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). The LG matrix was combined to an amino acid class frequency mixture model with 20 (for single gene trees) and 40 (for concatenated datasets) frequency component profiles. Statistical support for branches was assessed by multiparametric bootstrapping (1000 replicates) in RAxML and by the ultrafast bootstrap approximation (UFboot) with 1000 replicates in IQ-TREE.

passages.section: MATERIALS AND METHODS > Substitution rate and phylogenetic analyses
passages.text: The level of base substitution saturation for each gene and each position of the PCGs was assessed using DAMBE 5.6.14 (Xia, 2013). Substitution of each of the three codon positions are generally not saturated, except for the transition of 3rd codon positions (Figure S1). Therefore, the 3rd codon positions of PCGs were excluded for the phylogenetic analyses. Each gene was aligned using MAFFT 7.402 (Katoh & Standley, 2013) with algorithm G‐INS‐i strategy. Gap in each matrix was treated as the fifth character and was retained in this study. Alignments of individual genes were then concatenated using SequenceMatrix v1.7.8 (Vaidya et al., 2011), after which three datasets were prepared for phylogenetic analyses: PCG12 (the 1st and 2nd codon positions of the 13 PCGs), PCG12R (the 1st and 2nd codon positions of the 13 PCGs and two rRNAs), and third AA (amino acid sequences of the 13 PCGs). The best partitioning scheme and best‐fit substitution model for each partition was tested using PartitionFinder 2.0 (Lanfear et al., 2017) with the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). Phylogenetic analyses were conducted with Maximum likelihood (ML) reconstruction and Bayesian inference (BI). The ML analysis was performed using IQ‐TREE 1.6.10 (Nguyen et al., 2015) with the best‐fit substitution model and 1000 bootstrap replicates. BI analysis was performed using MrBayes 3.2.7a (Ronquist et al., 2012) with substitution model in Table S1. Two simultaneous Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) runs of 10,000,000 generations were conducted, trees were sampled every 1000 generations, and the first 25% of trees discarded as burn‐in. Tracer 1.7 (Rambaut et al., 2018) was used to check convergence of runs.

Although there are numerous programs that can concatenate matrices at the multilocus scale (e.g., 2matrix [Salinas and Little, 2014], SequenceMatrix [Vaidya et al., 2011], iPhy [Jones et al., 2011], AIR‐appender [Kumar et al., 2009]), input datasets for phylogenomic analyses of eukaryotes are typically one to two orders of magnitude larger than would be used in even the largest traditional multilocus phylogenetic datasets. Accordingly, few publicly available, stand‐alone programs (e.g., SCaFoS [Roure et al., 2007], IQ‐TREE [Minh et al., 2020], Phyx [Brown et al., 2017]) can accomplish the concatenation task on a genomic scale. Furthermore, most programs omit a substantial amount of genetic data while composing their matrices, namely, insertions/deletions (indels) and gene content (presence/absence); morphology is also often ignored in phylogenomic tools. Additionally, most phylogenomic practitioners remove genes from the concatenated matrix that have not been recovered for a set proportion (e.g., 25–50%) of the terminal organisms (Philippe et al., 2004; Roure et al., 2013; Streicher et al., 2016)—a process we will refer to as occupancy filtering. At a phylogenomic scale, analytic efficiency is also critically important and can be improved by reducing problematic or unnecessary portions of the data. For example, removing loci with missing data typically increases efficiency, and parsimony analyses are made much more efficient by the removal of parsimony uninformative characters during matrix construction.

passages.text: The phylogenetic relationships were reconstructed by utilizing 13 protein-coding genes (PCGs) obtained from 25 sequences, including 4 newly sequenced A. bipustulatus mitogenomes. To provide a comprehensive reference dataset, complete or near-complete Dytiscidae mitochondrial genomes were downloaded from GenBank (Supplementary Table S2). Given that the Hydroporinae is the most numerous and diverse subfamily within Dytiscidae, we selected only 1 to 2 sequences from each tribe and/or subtribe in order to avoid an oversampling of this subfamily in comparison with others in the quantitative ratio. The 19 sequences were downloaded, representing 6 subfamilies: Dytiscinae (3), Cybistrinae (1), Agabinae (2), Colymbetinae (1), Copelatinae (1), and Hydroporinae (11). The selection of these specific references was based on their close evolutionary relationship to A. bipustulatus, as established by the most recent and comprehensive phylogenetic analyses of diving beetles (Ribera et al. 2008, Villastrigo et al. 2021, Miller and Bergsten 2023). Additionally, two outgroup sequences, Hygrobia hermanni (KT876898) and Carabus lafossei (KY992943), were included based on their prior use in studies by Nagata (2019) and Vasconcelos et al. (2021). Our analysis was conducted using only 13 PCG sequences, thus excluding those of rRNA genes and the control region (CR), because the latter had heterogeneous length among the reference genomes. To date, the majority of other phylogenetic studies utilizing mitogenome data have predominantly relied on 13 PCGs, an approach that we have also employed in our analysis. Each PCG sequence was individually aligned using the online MAFFT v7 tool with default settings and the L-INS-i algorithm (Katoh et al. 2019). The aligned sequences were then concatenated using SequenceMatrix (Vaidya et al. 2011). The selection of the best model was done using the ModelFinder of IQ-TREE (Nguyen et al. 2015, Kalyaanamoorthy et al. 2017). Maximum Likelihood (ML) phylogenetic trees were reconstructed using the raxmlGUI interface v2.0.10 and RAxML-NG with 100 bootstrap replicates (Edler et al. 2021). Bayesian inference (BI) analyses were performed in MrBayes v3.2 (Ronquist et al. 2012). Two independent Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) chains were run for 1,000,000 generations, sampling every 1,000 generations, with a 25% burn-in. Finally, the resulting phylogenetic tree was visualized with the Tree Visualization By One Table web tool (tvBOT) developed by Xie et al. (2023).

structure.abstract: We present SequenceMatrix, software that is designed to facilitate the assembly and analysis of multi-gene datasets. Genes are concatenated by dragging and dropping FASTA, NEXUS, or TNT files with aligned sequences into the program window. A multi-gene dataset is concatenated and displayed in a spreadsheet; each sequence is represented by a cell that provides information on sequence length, number of indels, the number of ambiguous bases ("Ns"), and the availability of codon information. Alternatively, GenBank numbers for the sequences can be displayed and exported. Matrices with hundreds of genes and taxa can be concatenated within minutes and exported in TNT, NEXUS, or PHYLIP formats, preserving both character set and codon information for TNT and NEXUS files. SequenceMatrix also creates taxon sets listing taxa with a minimum number of characters or gene fragments, which helps assess preliminary datasets. Entire taxa, whole gene fragments, or individual sequences for a particular gene and species can be excluded from export. Data matrices can be re-split into their component genes and the gene fragments can be exported as individual gene files. SequenceMatrix also includes two tools that help to identify sequences that may have been compromised through laboratory contamination or data management error. One tool lists identical or near-identical sequences within genes, while the other compares the pairwise distance pattern of one gene against the pattern for all remaining genes combined. SequenceMatrix is Java-based and compatible with the Microsoft Windows, Apple MacOS X and Linux operating systems. The software is freely available from http://code.google.com/p/sequencematrix/. © The Willi Hennig Society 2010.

points.text: The core claim — fast concatenation of individually aligned gene files into a single multi-gene supermatrix — is exactly what 39 of 40 citers use it for, almost always as a one-line methods step before phylogenetic inference (e.g. 67 plastid protein-coding genes, 79 nuclear+mitochondrial partitions, seven housekeeping genes for MLST).

Preservation of character set and codon information across the round trip is picked up by only a small minority: one citer explicitly specifies codon partitions in the exported supermatrix and another exports in NEXUS format. The claim that partition metadata survives is confirmed in practice but rarely worth mentioning to citers.

Several citers use it as a general alignment-management/editing utility rather than a concatenator proper — editing sequence names, 'manually combining trimmed alignments', or concatenating 14 already-aligned protein sequences — housekeeping the paper never advertised as its selling point.

One citer concatenates just two loci (ITS2 + rbcLa, and elsewhere cox1+cox2, SSU+cox1, CO1+EF1α). The paper's pitch was matrices with hundreds of genes and taxa assembled in minutes; a large share of real use is two- to six-gene datasets where speed is irrelevant and the tool is chosen for convenience and format export.

The contamination- and error-flagging tools — the stated conclusion that users can 'catch data-management errors before analysis' via pairwise distance checks and flagged sequences — appear in none of the 40 sampled uses. Citers treat the program purely as a file-joining step, not as a QC gate.

Generated taxon sets for assessing preliminary datasets by completeness threshold, and the reversibility of concatenation back into component gene files, are never invoked. No citer reports splitting a matrix or using completeness-based taxon selection.

Cross-platform Java accessibility is a stated conclusion but is invisible in citation practice; the single non-methods citation is a background mention positioning SequenceMatrix as one of the existing concatenation tools that motivated BAD2matrix, not as a portability or accessibility benchmark.
